attacks_command: python attacks/<script>.py, run from this run directory; each writes its own JSON beside itself. DEADLOCK_CLAIM.md section 7 says what each one attacked and which numbers it broke.

determinism.fd_numbers_are_not_reconstructible_from_: Every Fast Downward number in this run came from a binary that is not tracked by git and cannot be rebuilt from the repository alone. The repo's byte-reproducibility requirement does not cover them. What replaces it is the hash, commit and build command below: a rebuild that hashes differently is a question a reader can raise.
determinism.ipdb_expansion_counts_are_measured_but_a: DEADLOCK_CLAIM.md section 7b withdraws them: iPDB's pattern generation moves the count by more than the effect under study. They are re-derived on a fixed task, where that lottery cannot bite, but no conclusion in the document rests on an ipdb row.
determinism.structural_results_are_reproducible: Node counts, generated and evaluated counts, initial heuristic values, plan lengths, translator task sizes and exit codes are a function of the instance and the configuration. audit/verify.py re-derives a subset -- far4 blind before/after and every dead-start instance -- and compares them exactly.
determinism.the_set_results_need_no_planner_at_all: The three sets of DEADLOCK_CLAIM.md section 3 (truly dead, relaxation dead, theorem dead) are pure Python over the reachable space, and so is the rnd0021 counterexample of section 3a. audit/verify.py regenerates rnd0021 from attacks/a3_family.py's random_level(seed=20260728) and recomputes its numbers rather than reading them, so that check runs on a machine that has never built a planner.
determinism.timings_are_not: Every wall-clock figure here is a property of this machine at this moment. audit/verify.py checks that timings are present, non-negative and no larger than the run they sit inside; it never compares them for equality, and neither should a reader.

notes: DEADLOCK_CLAIM.md is listed in files[] as ../../DEADLOCK_CLAIM.md. It lives in engine-rig/, not in this run directory, but it is the artefact the run exists to support, and a hash on it is what keeps the document and its evidence from drifting apart -- which they did twice before the current draft.

Three numbers this run originally published were broken by its own adversarial reviewers and are withdrawn in DEADLOCK_CLAIM.md section 7: the far8 and far9 ipdb dividends, n_theorem_dead_outside_relaxation = 0 read as a statement about the encoding rather than about the far{N} family, and the 'redundant, not unused' explanation of the zero.

attacks/a6_subsets.py and attacks/a2b_ipdb_repeat.py wrote no output and attacks/a7_hunt.py was killed at 71 of a planned 400 instances. Section 7d records that; the absence of their JSON from files[] is that fact, not an omission from this manifest.

toolchain.re_derived_not_copied: This block was probed from the live binary when the manifest was completed, not copied from E2's manifest. audit/verify.py compares binary_sha256 against the planner in front of it before it re-measures anything, so a structural comparison cannot quietly be made against a different build.
toolchain.reproducibility_gap: Every Fast Downward number in this run came from a binary that is not tracked by git and cannot be rebuilt from the repository alone. The repo's byte-reproducibility requirement does not cover them. What replaces it is the hash, commit and build command below: a rebuild that hashes differently is a question a reader can raise.
toolchain.why_not_in_the_repository: .toolchain/ is gitignored by design (~1.6 GB of compiler, planner and build tree). See P-13.

why_the_directories_are_not_hashed_file_: Those directories hold 1232 raw Fast Downward logs and several thousand generated PDDL files. A hash for each would run to thousands of entries and make this manifest unreadable, which is the opposite of what a manifest is for. Every conclusion in DEADLOCK_CLAIM.md is drawn from the JSON in files[], and that IS hashed file by file; the logs are the raw material those JSON files were parsed out of, kept so a reader can re-parse them rather than trust the parser. The log counts are recorded here so that a wholesale deletion is at least visible.
